newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Red tape curls into Zaire rebel territory.
newsitem.headline: Red tape curls into Zaire rebel territory.

text.p: Faced with running a slice of conquered land, Zairean rebels have simply adopted the administration already in place despite its reputation for inefficiency and corruption.

The rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) say they are fighting to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko whose 31-year rule has pauperised a nation whose mineral wealth could have made it one of the richest in Africa.
In three months the rebels have carved a narrow slice of land from Zaire's eastern border over 500 kms (300 miles) long, occupying the major eastern towns of Goma and Bukavu.
But the rebel liberation has changed little in the way the system was run by Mobutu's henchmen.
Step into the new passport office in Goma and a visitor could be forgiven for thinking nothing had changed in the dark and crowded corridors.
Paperwork has piled ever higher as people rush to replace now useless Zairean identity cards with passes from "The Democratic Republic of Congo".
"The system is the same, but the methods are different," rebel leader Laurent Kabila told Reuters.
"We cannnot expel everybody at once because there would be chaos."
And as rebel fighters have gone deeper into the forests and hills government offices have steadily reopened in Goma.
Old files have been dug out and new forms printed where the only difference is the change from Zaire to Congo, the name given by Belgian colonialists and changed by Mobutu to erase the colonial past.
Even at the internal intelligence headquarters only the big bosses who fled before the rebel advance have been replaced -- most of the agents are doing the same jobs as before.

"There has been a noticeable change in dealing with the bureaucracy, it doesn't cost as much as it did and the charges seem more official than they were. At least for the moment," said one expatriate worker in Goma.
But Kabila has asked civil servants to work without pay for the good of the "revolution".
They will remain unpaid until the new rulers can find enough money by exploiting the mineral and agricultural wealth in the occupied territory, which include gold and coffee.
And with a war to fight, civil adminstration is unlikely to be the first priority for spending scarce funds.

Used to going without salaries for months on end, Zaire's public officials have always risen to their financial challenge with alacrity -- imposing strictly unofficial charges for every service in a system of institutional corruption.
With at least 600,000 civil servants for a country of over 40 million people, successive governments in Kinshasa either fuelled hyperinflation by printing money to pay them or simply didn't bother.

Western-backed reforms introduced by Kinshasa's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo aimed at cutting the public sector and dismantling the corrupt system have had little effect but to hurt his own popularity.

"Only those of us who have some integrity are allowed to continue work," said Felicien Samosha, an inspector at the customs office in Goma, whose staff is virtually unchanged since the rebel takeover.
"But it is not easy to live when we are not paid and we cannot feed our families. If we have to go much longer without pay it really will make it impossible to do our job properly."
